content.p: The Vineland Boys were a street gang based in the San Fernando Valley of Los Angeles. Federal prosecutors placed their territory in Sun Valley, North Hollywood and Burbank. The gang was known for selling methamphetamine, extorting drug dealers and shooting at rivals, and it became the subject of two large federal crackdowns, one of them begun after the killing of a Burbank police officer in November 2003.

The gang's name came from Vineland Street in North Hollywood, where its early members played football. Its history runs from a robbery in 1988 to a string of federal convictions that continued after 2019, and it shows how a neighborhood crew grew into a racketeering case that ran from street shootings to a former councilwoman's home.
content.h2: A crew with a neighborhood name
content.p: Police Magazine's account of the gang says it was formed in the mid-1980s by young men who had been members or associates of the 18th Street Gang. The 18th Street Gang treated the new group as a breakaway and the two sides fought for years. The magazine says the founders included Teddy Lopez, known as "Green Eyes," and his brother Hilario Lopez.

In January 1988, according to the same account, Teddy Lopez, then in the ninth grade, and about ten to twelve other young members set out on a robbery that ended in the killing of a 26-year-old man, Carlos Cardoza. The gang's criminal activity led its members in and out of juvenile facilities in Los Angeles, the magazine says.

The Los Angeles Times reported in 2003 that the gang was also tied to a shooting of a police officer more than a decade before. In 1988, according to LAPD officials quoted by the paper, a 16-year-old gang member named Robert Steele shot rookie officer James Beyea during a burglary arrest in North Hollywood. About three hours later, officers killed Steele, saying he had brandished Beyea's service revolver.
content.h2: The green light and the rivals
content.p: The Mexican Mafia, a prison gang that set rules for Hispanic street gangs in Southern California, judged the Vineland Boys by its rules. Police Magazine says the group broke the traditional rules and was placed under a "green light," which made its members targets for other Sureño gangs. The Los Angeles Times, quoting Officer Dan Fournier of the Los Angeles Police Department's North Hollywood Division, said the green light arose in the early 1990s after the gang kept back part of its drug profits, and that it lasted four or five years.

During that period, the paper reported, any member who went to jail or prison could be attacked, and rival street gangs could target Vineland members in drive-by shootings. The gang then changed its style, dropping shaved heads, baggy clothes and large tattoos, and it kept a low profile. The paper said the gang's penchant for anonymity arose out of necessity.

Police Magazine says that about ten years after the gang formed, Teddy Lopez was attacked with knives and beer bottles at Baby Doe's night club in Monterey Park, where other people recognized him as marked for death. The magazine reports that some of the suspects yelled "Surenos!" and "Pacoima!" as they murdered him. The Los Angeles Times also linked the gang to the 1998 killing of Saul Santiago, a teenager from San Fernando High School who had no gang ties, and reported that a Vineland member, Juan Corral, was sentenced to more than 100 years in prison for it.

Police Magazine says the gang then tried to repair its relations with the Mexican Mafia, became more reckless in its violence and made alliances with the Armenian Power gang to obtain assault weapons. It describes the group's main business in that period as the distribution of large amounts of methamphetamine.

On 15 November 2003, Burbank police officer Gregory Campbell noticed two men sitting in a car without license plates in the lot of a Ramada Inn near Burbank Airport, in an area then known for drug and gang activity. Campbell radioed for help, and his partner, Matthew Pavelka, arrived as backup. According to the Crescenta Valley Weekly, the two men in the vehicle, David Garcia and Ramon Aranda, then opened fire on the officers. Both officers were hit. Pavelka, 26, was killed. Aranda, 25, was also killed. Garcia ran off.

The Los Angeles Times described Pavelka as a 26-year-old rookie officer and the son of an LAPD detective, and noted that he was the first Burbank officer to be shot dead while on duty. The paper said Garcia, then 19, and Aranda, 25, opened fire as the officers approached the vehicle. Campbell's injuries are described differently. Police Magazine's 2007 account says he was paralyzed. The Los Angeles Times in 2003, Police Magazine in 2012 and the Crescenta Valley Weekly describe him as wounded.

The manhunt drew large numbers of officers. The Los Angeles Times reported that as many as 1,000 officers took part in sweeps of the northeast San Fernando Valley, and that authorities arrested more than 60 of Garcia's friends and family, roughly a third were held on suspicion of aiding the fugitive. Garcia's twin brother, James Garcia, and a neighbor were charged as accessories after the fact of murder and pleaded not guilty. The paper said the search crossed the border, with investigators in Los Angeles and Tijuana sharing information.

Garcia was arrested on Thanksgiving Day 2003 in a neighborhood near Tijuana. Police found methamphetamine, an assault rifle and a submachine gun in the vehicle, and Los Angeles County prosecutors later charged him with capital murder and attempted murder. On 24 July 2012, Garcia pleaded guilty in Los Angeles Superior Court to first-degree murder, to the attempted murder of Campbell and to several weapons and drug counts. Judge Robert J. Perry sentenced him to life in prison without the possibility of parole. The plea included two special circumstances: that the victim was a peace officer on duty, and that the killing was done to avoid a lawful arrest.

Police Magazine says that in June 2005 a task force of 1,300 officers and agents from six local police agencies, the FBI, the DEA, the U.S. Marshals Service and the Internal Revenue Service carried out Operation Silent Night against the Vineland Boys. The federal indictment that followed named 49 defendants, and it charged the gang's members under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act.

The first trial ended on 27 October 2006. A DEA news release said nine members and associates were convicted that day, and that seven of them were found to have taken part in a racketeering enterprise that was responsible, among other things, for the murder of a Burbank police officer. The statement said 36 defendants had by then been convicted of federal charges. Police Magazine reported in 2007 that more than 35 members were convicted over two years, and that the gang's leader, Rafael Yepiz, was given a life sentence.

The case also reached into the Burbank city government. Stacey Jo Murphy, a former Burbank city councilwoman, was the subject of a police warrant served at her home in July 2005, which found cocaine in her bedroom and three semi-automatic handguns with 700 rounds of ammunition in the garage. Her longtime boyfriend, Scott Schaffer, had already pleaded guilty to federal gun charges, and investigators believed he had given his registered handgun to the gang in return for narcotics. Burbank police Sgt. Jay Jette said neither Murphy nor Schaffer was a member of the Vineland Boys.

In December 2005, Murphy pleaded guilty to felony cocaine possession and to a misdemeanor count of child endangerment, after the guns had been found in a garage her 12-year-old son used for play. The Los Angeles Times reported that she received five years' probation and entered a drug diversion program, with no jail time. The paper said she had to show she had enrolled in drug and parenting classes. The Los Angeles County district attorney's office called the deal "an appropriate resolution" of the case.

A San Mateo newspaper, which also reported the plea, gave Murphy's former role as "mayor of Burbank" rather than councilwoman. The same report said that if she failed to finish the program she could face up to three years in prison on the felony and six months in jail on the misdemeanor. If she completed it, she could ask the court to dismiss the case.

On 13 February 2019, federal agents arrested 25 members and associates of the Vineland Boys. The Justice Department said 11 defendants were already in custody and that nine fugitives were still being sought, four of them believed to be in Mexico. Five federal grand jury indictments named 45 defendants in all. The main indictment alleged that 31 members and associates had taken part in a criminal enterprise and conspired to violate the RICO Act.

The indictment alleged that the gang, to control its territory in Sun Valley, North Hollywood and Burbank, shot and assaulted rivals, ran drug and gun trafficking and extorted money from drug dealers as "taxes". It also detailed an April 2016 episode on Lankershim Boulevard in which gunfire hit a member of a rival gang, and it said that one defendant who was not a gang member allegedly made untraceable AR-15-type rifles with no serial numbers, known as ghost guns, which, authorities said, were sold to gang members who were barred from owning firearms. Other indictments charged 14 people with supplying methamphetamine to the gang, and some of those transactions were said to have taken place near an elementary school.

U.S. Attorney Nick Hanna, speaking at a news conference, said the earlier prosecutions had dealt the gang a blow, but that "over the ensuing years a new generation of Vineland Boys emerged." NBC Los Angeles reported that the same day's operation also targeted a separate South Los Angeles gang, Florencia-13. The Justice Department said the 2019 indictments followed a 2005 operation that had produced "more than four dozen convictions." That figure is higher than the 36 convictions the 2006 statement gave, and the two statements were made at different times.

Jesus Gonzalez Jr., described by prosecutors as a member of the Sun Valley group, pleaded guilty on 22 January to five felonies, including conspiracy under the RICO Act, two counts of violent crime in aid of racketeering and a firearms count. Prosecutors said he took part in the attempted murders of three rival gang members. A 2016 drive-by shooting outside a party in Sun Valley, and a later shooting on Lankershim Boulevard in North Hollywood, were among the incidents that prosecutors described. Judge Michael W. Fitzgerald sentenced him to 372 months, which is 31 years, in federal prison. Gangsters Inc. reported that he also sold methamphetamine and illegally sold guns, including a ghost gun, outside a McDonald's in San Fernando.

Mario Alberto Miranda, the lead defendant in the 2019 indictment, was sentenced to 192 months in federal prison, or 16 years. Prosecutors said he pleaded guilty to a RICO conspiracy and to a conspiracy to distribute methamphetamine. From at least September 2008 to November 2019, they said, he supplied drugs within the gang's territory, ran stash houses, extorted drug dealers and, as the gang's "shot caller," ordered members to attack rivals and people suspected of cooperating with police.

The prosecutors' statements on the later case give varying totals. Gangsters Inc. reported 17 convictions and several prison terms of more than 10 years in the case at the time of Gonzalez's sentence, while the ATF's account of Miranda's sentence said 30 guilty pleas had been secured, 19 of them leading to sentences of at least 10 years. It also said one defendant had died after being indicted. The Los Angeles Times called the gang a 300-member group in 2003; the reports quoted here give no later membership figure.
content.h2: What the figures do and do not show
content.p: The available accounts agree on the main points: the gang was formed in the mid-1980s, it clashed with the 18th Street Gang and was placed under a Mexican Mafia green light, Officer Pavelka was killed in 2003 by Garcia, who later pleaded guilty, and federal prosecutors brought two large racketeering cases, in 2005 and 2019. They differ on the numbers. Police Magazine's account of the first trial and the Justice Department's later figures count convictions at different times. Campbell's injuries are described as paralysis in one report, Police Magazine's 2007 account, and as wounds in three others.

The 2019 indictments remain allegations in the indictments themselves. Those named in them were presumed innocent unless proven guilty, and the convictions described above relate to the defendants named in the press releases quoted here, not to every person arrested in 2019. The outcome of the remaining cases is not described in the reports quoted above.
